title: The Schoolmaster's Integral: Beauvais, Nancy, and the Measure of Scattered Points
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Beauvais, the birth in the rue de la Madeleine
stops.date_confidence: Date and city attested (MacTutor; fr.wikipedia): 28 June 1875, Beauvais, Oise. The street address, 29 rue de la Madeleine, rests on a citation of the Archives departementales de l'Oise civil register that could not be re-fetched. The research pool carried two different longitudes for the same house, 2.0808 and 2.087, and neither lands on the street; the pin here is Nominatim's main stretch of the rue de la Madeleine, 49.4296, 2.0831. The house itself is not identified.
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of June a son is born in Beauvais to Éloi Léon Lebesgue, a typographer, and Marie Estelle Amélie Leclerc, a seamstress; they register him Léon Henri. Beauvais is a cathedral town sixty miles north of Paris, in the Oise, its choir the tallest in France and its nave never built. The house is gone, and the number survives only through an archive citation that nobody has been able to check again. What the citation gives is an address in the rue de la Madeleine, a street that runs out of the centre toward Voisinlieu.
suggested_refs: The rue de la Madeleine, Beauvais, and the civil register of the Archives departementales de l'Oise

stops.name: Beauvais, the house emptied by tuberculosis
stops.date_confidence: Year only, and even that is inferred. MacTutor and en.wikipedia have the father dying while Lebesgue was young; fr.wikipedia states that the father and Lebesgue's two elder sisters all died of tuberculosis when he was three, which puts it in 1878 or 1879. A precise date of 14 April 1879 appears in the research pool from an unverified civil-register citation and is not used here. Month and day default to January.
stops.campa: He is three when tuberculosis takes the household apart. The French account is flat about it: the typographer father and both elder sisters die of it in the same season, and what is left is a widow and a boy. Marie Leclerc keeps them by sewing; the poverty is not in dispute, and neither are the lungs. Some later summaries have an elder sister helping to support the house through his school years, which cannot stand if the sisters are already dead. The sources contradict each other here, and the contradiction is left standing.
suggested_refs: The Beauvais civil death registers for 1878-1879, not located in this research

stops.name: Beauvais, the collège
stops.date_confidence: Attendance at the College de Beauvais is attested (MacTutor). No start year is given anywhere reachable; 1885 is a placeholder chosen to sit inside the 1880s, with month and day defaulted. The pin is a town-centre approximation, and the modern successor school, the Lycee Felix Faure, stands further out at 49.4352, 2.0898 and is deliberately not used.
stops.campa: He is sent to the Collège de Beauvais, the town's secondary school, where the masters find in a seamstress's son the one thing a seamstress's son has no way of converting into a living: he is very good at mathematics. Within a few years his teachers are willing to tell the municipality of Beauvais, in writing, that this boy should not be allowed to stop. Of his own work in the building nothing survives. No exercise book, and no prize list that anyone has produced.
suggested_refs: The College de Beauvais, absorbed into the later Lycee Felix Faure

stops.name: Beauvais, the Hôtel de Ville and the Bourse Chevalier
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The award of the Bourse Chevalier on 24 May 1889 comes from printed municipal council deliberations reported by the director of the Oise departmental archives in 1991; the 1889 register itself was not located, and the original scholarship dossiers were destroyed in the bombing of Beauvais in June 1940. The research pool tagged this claim attested in one array and reconstruction in the other; the weaker tag is taken. Coordinate corrected to Nominatim's Hotel de Ville, 49.4295, 2.0812, the pool's figure sitting some 500 m north of the building.
stops.campa: His widowed mother petitions the town for a college scholarship, and on the twenty-fourth of May the municipal council votes her son the vacant Bourse Chevalier, recording that the information gathered about the boy was very favorable. It is the scholarship that puts a typographer's son on the Paris train, and a second award will follow in 1893 to carry him through his last year there. The papers that would prove any of it burned in June 1940, when German bombing took the archives of Beauvais along with most of the town centre.
suggested_refs: The printed deliberations of the Beauvais municipal council, 24 May 1889, as reported by the Oise departmental archive director in 1991
sources: Research dossier's citation of the printed Beauvais council deliberations (register not located)

stops.name: Paris, the Lycée Saint-Louis
stops.date_confidence: Attendance attested (MacTutor; fr.wikipedia). No year is given for the move to Paris. The research pool dated it 1889 and placed it in Paris, which conflates the Beauvais college years with the Paris lycees; the early 1890s is the most that can be said, and 1891 is a placeholder with month and day defaulted. Coordinate corrected to Nominatim's Lycee Saint-Louis at 44 boulevard Saint-Michel, 48.8490, 2.3415, about 150 m from the pool's figure.
stops.campa: He crosses to Paris and enters the Lycée Saint-Louis on the boulevard Saint-Michel, a scholarship boy from the Oise among the sons of the capital. Saint-Louis has one business, the preparation of candidates for the competitive examinations of the grandes écoles, and from about the age of fifteen that is what he is: a candidate, drilled daily against a date. From these years nothing of his own has been found: no letter, no notebook, and no schoolfellow's recollection of what he was like to sit beside.
suggested_refs: The Lycee Saint-Louis, 44 boulevard Saint-Michel, Paris

stops.name: Paris, the Lycée Louis-le-Grand
stops.date_confidence: Attendance attested (MacTutor; fr.wikipedia). The second Bourse Chevalier, dated 15 September 1893 in the research pool, and the council record of his thanks on 28 September 1894, come from the same unverified printed deliberations as the first award and are reconstruction. Month and day default to January. Coordinate corrected to Nominatim's Lycee Louis-le-Grand, 48.8479, 2.3450, about 230 m from the pool's figure.
stops.campa: A second Bourse Chevalier from Beauvais moves him along the rue Saint-Jacques into Louis-le-Grand, and into the special mathematics class that prepares the science section of the École normale supérieure. The examination he is being drilled for admits a few dozen men in the sciences for the whole of France each year, and everything after it depends on one week in a hall. The council at home, according to the printed deliberations, receives his thanks the following September.
suggested_refs: The Lycee Louis-le-Grand, rue Saint-Jacques, Paris, and its classe de mathematiques speciales
sources: Research dossier's citation of the Beauvais council award of 15 September 1893 (not verified)

stops.name: Paris, entry to the École normale supérieure
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (MacTutor; en.wikipedia): entry to the ENS in 1894. The month is the ordinary start of the French academic year and is inferred; the day is defaulted. The often-repeated rank of fifth in the cohort is not in MacTutor or in either Wikipedia, and is treated as tradition, so it stays out of the prose. Paul Langevin and Paul Montel entering the same year is plausible and likewise unsourced in the pool. Coordinate from Nominatim, 48.8417, 2.3448.
stops.campa: He enters the École normale supérieure in the rue d'Ulm at nineteen. The school exists to make secondary schoolmasters, and that is what it makes of him first: three years later he is qualified, and two years after that he is teaching in a lycée in Lorraine. It is also, in the 1890s, the building in which Émile Borel and René Baire are taking the calculus apart at the joints, and discovering as they go that nobody can say what the size of an arbitrary set of points is.
suggested_refs: The Ecole normale superieure, 45 rue d'Ulm, Paris

stops.name: Paris, the Sorbonne and the teaching diploma
stops.date_confidence: The 1897 teaching diploma is attested (MacTutor). Month and day are not recorded and default to January. The frequently repeated claim that he placed third in the agregation de mathematiques is not in MacTutor, which does not mention the agregation at all, and is demoted to tradition. The Sorbonne pin 48.8496, 2.3442 is the corpus's corrected pin for 47 rue des Ecoles and is inherited byte for byte rather than re-derived.
stops.campa: The teaching diploma comes in 1897, and with it the right to teach mathematics in a French lycée. He does not leave Paris. He is twenty-two, licensed to be a schoolmaster, and instead of taking a post he stays on two more years to read in a library, on money voted by a town council in the Oise on the strength of a report that the boy was worth it. Tradition adds that he placed third in the agrégation. The rank turns up in every short account of him; the record that gives the diploma does not mention the agrégation at all.
suggested_refs: The Faculte des sciences de Paris, 47 rue des Ecoles

stops.name: Paris, two years in the school library
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the span 1897-1899 (MacTutor: he studied in the school's library, reading Baire's work on discontinuous functions). No single date attaches to it; 1898 sits inside the span, and month and day are defaulted. The fuller reading list, Jordan's content and Borel's measure alongside Baire, is the research pool's synthesis rather than a sourced inventory.
stops.campa: He stays on as a scholarship holder and reads. Camille Jordan's theory of content, Émile Borel's countably additive measure, René Baire's classification of the functions that jump everywhere: three unfinished attempts on one difficulty, which is that nobody can say what size to assign an arbitrary set of points on a line, and so nobody can say what the integral of a badly behaved function means. The men who wrote them are alive, and some of them are in the building. The record of the two years is one line: that he read in the school's library, and read Baire there on the discontinuous functions.
suggested_refs: Rene Baire's thesis on discontinuous functions (1899); Emile Borel's Lecons sur la theorie des fonctions (1898); Camille Jordan's Cours d'analyse

stops.name: Paris, the first paper
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (en.wikipedia, list of major publications): Sur l'approximation des fonctions, 1898. No month or day is recorded and both default to January. The pin is the corpus's canonical Paris pin, 48.8566, 2.3522, used because no place of composition is recorded anywhere reached.
stops.campa: His first paper appears, on the approximation of functions. It is the work of a young licensed schoolmaster putting a note where notes are put, and nobody reading it in 1898 would have marked the author. Nothing in it announces the thing that is three years off. The great French mathematics of the decade is being made by men with chairs, and he has a classroom. Between this paper and the four pages of 1901 lie the library in the rue d'Ulm, a move east into Lorraine, and a lycée timetable of a dozen hours a week in front of boys.
suggested_refs: Lebesgue, 'Sur l'approximation des fonctions' (1898)

segments.name: Nancy, and the Note of April 1901

stops.name: Nancy, the lycée
stops.date_confidence: Attested (MacTutor): professor at the Lycee Centrale, Nancy, 1899-1902. October 1899 as the start month is more precise than any source reached and is inferred from the French academic year; the day is defaulted. Coordinate corrected to Nominatim's Lycee Henri-Poincare, Nancy, 48.6910, 6.1787, about 430 m from the figure in the research pool.
stops.campa: He goes to Lorraine as professor of mathematics at the lycée in Nancy and teaches secondary school for three years. In those three years he does the work his name will carry. Everything in the subject before him had taken the domain of a function and chopped it finer and finer; he arrives at twenty-four and leaves at twenty-seven with an answer written down that chops the other axis instead. There is no institute behind him and no laboratory, no assistant and no supervisor leaning over the page. There is a timetable, a provincial town in Lorraine, and the question of what an integral is.
suggested_refs: The Lycee Centrale at Nancy, now the Lycee Henri-Poincare

stops.name: Paris, the note of the twenty-ninth of April
stops.date_confidence: Attested (MacTutor; en.wikipedia): the note Sur une generalisation de l'integrale definie was presented to the Academie des sciences on 29 April 1901 and printed in Comptes rendus 132, 1025-1028. The pin is the Institut de France, seat of the Academie, where the note was read; Lebesgue was posted at Nancy and it is not established that he was in the room. The money-counting letter to Paul Montel carries no date in any source reached.
stops.campa: The Comptes rendus of the Académie des sciences carries four pages from a lycée professor at Nancy. Riemann had cut the domain into thin strips and summed the areas. Lebesgue cuts the other way: he gathers all the points at which the function's value falls between two levels, however scattered those points are, measures that set, and sums. Functions too broken for Riemann's method become integrable, and a limit can be taken inside the integral sign under conditions that finally hold. The note is four pages long.
stops.quote: I have to pay a certain sum... I take the bills and coins out of my pocket and give them to the creditor in the order I find them... This is the Riemann integral. But I can proceed differently... I order the bills and coins according to identical values and then I pay the several heaps one after the other... This is my integral.
stops.quote_source: Lebesgue to Paul Montel, letter, date not given in any source reached; quoted in Wikipedia, 'Lebesgue integration', after Siegmund-Schultze (2008).
suggested_refs: Comptes rendus de l'Academie des sciences 132 (1901), 1025-1028

stops.name: Paris, the doctorate for Intégrale, longueur, aire
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (MacTutor; en.wikipedia): doctorate from the Faculte des sciences de Paris in 1902, the thesis printed in the Annali di Matematica Pura ed Applicata at Milan. No month or day is recorded and both default to January. Sorbonne pin inherited byte for byte from the corpus, 48.8496, 2.3442.
stops.campa: The Faculté des sciences de Paris gives him the doctorate for Intégrale, longueur, aire, some hundred and thirty pages that turn the new integral on the oldest questions in the subject: what the length of a curve is, what the area of a surface is, when a function has a derivative, when a limit may be carried inside an integral. The thesis is not printed in Paris. It goes to Milan, into the Annali di Matematica pura ed applicata. He is twenty-seven.
suggested_refs: Lebesgue, 'Integrale, longueur, aire', Annali di Matematica Pura ed Applicata (Milan, 1902)

stops.name: Rennes, the first university post
stops.date_confidence: Attested (MacTutor): maitre de conferences at the Faculty of Science in Rennes from 1902, held until 1906. The month is inferred from the academic year and the day is defaulted. The coordinate is the research pool's figure for the old Faculte des sciences in central Rennes and was not challenged during verification.
stops.campa: He is made maître de conférences at the Faculté des sciences de Rennes and goes to Brittany. Four years of teaching analysis in a provincial faculty, with the doctorate done, the theory built, and no Paris post in sight. The French system moves men by seniority and by the votes of faculties, and the fact that a candidate has already changed what the word integral means does not shorten the queue by so much as a year. He lodges in a house in the rue Pongérard.
suggested_refs: The house at 4 rue Pongerard, Rennes, later marked with a commemorative plaque

stops.name: Paris, the first Cours Peccot
stops.date_confidence: Attested (MacTutor): Cours Peccot lectures at the College de France in 1903 and again in 1905. No month or day is recorded for either series; both default to January.
stops.campa: The Cours Peccot is a lectureship at the Collège de France reserved for young mathematicians who have already done something. He is invited to give the first series and comes up from Rennes to lecture on integration and the search for primitive functions. In the room are the men who decide French appointments. He will publish the lectures the following year, and it is the book rather than the course that carries the method out of Paris. Who sat in the hall, and what was said afterwards, no account reached records.
suggested_refs: The Cours Peccot of the College de France, founded by the Peccot bequest for mathematicians under thirty

stops.name: Paris, the marriage to Louise Marguerite Vallet
stops.date_confidence: The date 3 December 1903 is attested (MacTutor). A civil-register marginal notation cited in the research pool gives 16 December instead, possibly distinguishing ceremony from registration; the discrepancy is printed and not resolved. Neither the 11th-arrondissement venue nor the bride's birth at Geneva is confirmed by anything reached, so the stop takes the corpus's canonical Paris pin, 48.8566, 2.3522, rather than the Mairie du 11e.
stops.campa: He marries Louise Marguerite Vallet, sister of a fellow student from the rue d'Ulm. He is twenty-eight, a maître de conférences at Rennes, lately invited to lecture at the Collège de France. Two dates for the wedding circulate, the third of December and the sixteenth, and nothing reached settles which is the ceremony and which is the clerk's entry; the arrondissement usually given for it is not confirmed either. What the record holds is a name, a month, two children to come, and a divorce thirteen years off that nobody wrote down a reason for.
suggested_refs: The Paris marriage registers for December 1903, not located in this research
sources: Research dossier's citation of an Oise civil-register marginal notation (not verified)

stops.name: Paris, the Leçons sur l'intégration
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (MacTutor's list of major publications): Lecons sur l'integration et la recherche des fonctions primitives, 1904, out of the first Cours Peccot. No month or day; both default to January. The canonical Paris pin is used, no place of composition being recorded.
stops.campa: The first Peccot course comes out as a book: Leçons sur l'intégration et la recherche des fonctions primitives. This is how the integral leaves four pages of a Comptes rendus note and becomes ordinary equipment; within twenty years the phrase Lebesgue integrable is in use by people with no idea that there is a living man attached to it. The book itself is short, and it is written so that a competent reader can follow the whole construction from the ground without taking anything on authority.
suggested_refs: Lebesgue, Lecons sur l'integration et la recherche des fonctions primitives (Gauthier-Villars, 1904)

stops.name: Paris, the second Cours Peccot
stops.date_confidence: Attested (MacTutor): the second Cours Peccot at the College de France in 1905. No month or day is recorded; both default to January. That the course became the Lecons sur les series trigonometriques of 1906 is stated by MacTutor; the attribution of the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma to this work is standard rather than verified against the text here.
stops.campa: He is invited back to the Collège de France for a second Peccot series, this one on trigonometric series. The problem is old and exact: when a function is written as an infinite sum of sines and cosines, when does the sum converge, and to what. Riemann's integral had left the question half answerable, and Lebesgue's answers it further. One of the results proved here, that the coefficients of an integrable function tend to zero, now travels under two surnames joined by a hyphen. The course comes out as a book the year after he gives it.
suggested_refs: The Riemann-Lebesgue lemma, standardly traced to the 1905 Peccot course and the 1906 book

stops.name: Paris, the Leçons sur les séries trigonométriques
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (MacTutor's list of major publications): Lecons sur les series trigonometriques, 1906, out of the second Cours Peccot. Month and day default to January. Joseph Fourier's Theorie analytique de la chaleur is dated 1822 from standard reference; the relation asserted here is Lebesgue's own engagement with Fourier series, not a documented statement by Lebesgue about Fourier the man.
stops.campa: The second book puts the new integral to the series Joseph Fourier had driven into the theory of heat eighty years before and could not make rigorous, because in 1822 the tools for saying what a sum of infinitely many sines means did not exist. Lebesgue's measure supplies them, and Fourier's coefficients, taken against the new integral, behave. Until now the theory has looked to most readers like a device built for pathological functions. Here it is turned on the analysis everybody was already doing, and it is the first large demonstration that it belongs there.
suggested_refs: Joseph Fourier, Theorie analytique de la chaleur (1822), the series Lebesgue's integration finally grounded

stops.name: Poitiers, chargé de cours
stops.date_confidence: Attested (MacTutor; en.wikipedia): appointed to the Faculty of Science at Poitiers in 1906, and there until 1910. November 1906 appears in the research pool with a precision MacTutor does not supply; October is likewise inferred here from the academic year and the day is defaulted, so the month should be read as uncertain either way. The coordinate is a Poitiers city-centre stand-in: the faculty building of 1906 is not identified, and the modern science campus at 46.6594, 0.3593 is the wrong site and is not used.
stops.campa: He moves from Brittany to Poitou as chargé de cours in mathematics. It is a step up and it is not Paris. He works on differentiation, on the Dirichlet problem, on Fredholm's integral equation; he is thirty-one, the integral is five years old and spreading through Germany and Italy, and he is teaching in a faculty of a few hundred students in a town on the Clain. Four years of this follow. Which building he lectured in has not been identified, and the faculty of 1906 has left no address anyone reached could give.
suggested_refs: The old Faculte des sciences de Poitiers, city centre, site not identified

stops.name: Poitiers, the chair of mechanics
stops.date_confidence: Attested (MacTutor): named professor of mechanics at Poitiers in 1907. No month or day is given anywhere reached; both default to January. The research pool's phrase 'the following November' is a precision MacTutor does not supply. Same city-centre coordinate as the previous stop, the faculty building being unidentified.
stops.campa: A year later he is named professor of mechanics at Poitiers. The title is not the one he wants and the subject is not the one he works in; a chair of mechanics is what a provincial faculty happens to have vacant, and he takes it. The measure theory goes on in whatever hours the mechanics course leaves him. In 1907 the outstanding French analyst of his generation is not teaching analysis at all. He is teaching statics and dynamics to young men who want to build things.
suggested_refs: The chair of mechanics at Poitiers, held 1907-1910

stops.name: Poitiers, the son
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The birth of a son, Jacques Charles Lebesgue, at Poitiers on 9 July 1908 comes from the research pool's citation of civil-record and biographical-dictionary material that could not be independently checked. Only the general outline is corroborated: that Lebesgue had two children and lived at Poitiers between 1906 and 1910. The coordinate is a Poitiers town pin; no address is known.
stops.campa: A son is born at Poitiers, Jacques Charles, who will grow up to teach at the lycée in Caen. There are two children of the marriage. Almost nothing else about the household is written down anywhere reached: no address, no description of the rooms, no letters between husband and wife on either side of the divorce that is eight years off. What survives of the private life is a name in a register and a count. The register itself has not been produced, and the date is carried on somebody else's word.
suggested_refs: The Poitiers civil birth registers for July 1908, not located in this research
sources: Research dossier's citation of civil-record data (not verified)

stops.name: Paris, back to the Sorbonne at last
stops.date_confidence: Year and post attested (MacTutor): appointed maitre de conferences in mathematical analysis at the Sorbonne in 1910. The precise day of 16 November 1910 that circulates in the research pool is not in MacTutor and could not be sourced elsewhere, so it is not used; month and day default to January. Sorbonne pin inherited byte for byte, 48.8496, 2.3442.
stops.campa: Eleven years after leaving the rue d'Ulm for a lycée in Nancy, he is brought back to Paris as maître de conférences in mathematical analysis at the Faculté des sciences. It is the post he has wanted since the doctorate, and it is a junior one: he is thirty-five, he holds no chair, and the promotion he assumes will follow does not follow. He lectures on analysis in the faculty that gave him the doctorate eight years earlier, for the work that made the analysis different. He will be a maître de conférences here for eight years more.
suggested_refs: The chair of mathematical analysis, Faculte des sciences de Paris

stops.name: Paris, one vote in thirty-five
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. That Lebesgue took a single vote out of thirty-five in a Sorbonne chair competition in 1912, and failed again in a faculty reorganisation, rests entirely on the research pool's account of Helene Gispert's archival work, which could not be fetched. The Prix Houllevigue of 1912 is separately attested (MacTutor). Month and day default to January.
stops.campa: A chair falls vacant and he stands for it. On the archival account he takes one vote out of thirty-five. In the same year the Institut gives him the Prix Houllevigue. The man whose integral is by now in every serious analysis course in Europe cannot persuade his own faculty to elect him a professor, and the same establishment that will not promote him hands him a prize for the work. The archival account of the ballot has not been checked at first hand, and the vote count stands on one historian's reading.
suggested_refs: Helene Gispert's archival work on the Paris faculty appointments of 1910-1918 (not fetched in this research)
sources: Research dossier's account of Gispert (not verified)

segments.name: The Firing Tables and the Quarrel

stops.name: Paris, the prizes of the Institut
stops.date_confidence: Attested (MacTutor's honours list; the Poncelet is also listed by en.wikipedia): Prix Houllevigue 1912, Prix Poncelet 1914, Prix Saintour 1917, Prix Petit d'Ormoy 1919. No months or days are recorded for any of them. The stop is dated 1914 to sit in the middle of the run, with month and day defaulted; it gathers four separate awards and does not mark one occasion.
stops.campa: Four prizes come from the Institut in eight years: Houllevigue in 1912, Poncelet in 1914, Saintour in 1917, Petit d'Ormoy in 1919. They are the currency in which the French mathematical establishment pays a man it has not promoted. Between the Poncelet and the Saintour there are three years in which he does no mathematics at all, because the state has him computing where shells will land. The chair arrives in 1918, and by then the friendship that opened the whole subject to him has ended in public. Each prize is announced by the Académie and carries a sum of money; none of them is a chair.
suggested_refs: The prize announcements of the Academie des sciences, 1912-1919

stops.name: Vitry-le-François, the firing tables
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The wartime work with Paul Montel on artillery firing tables under the inventions administration, coordinated with the Centre d'etudes d'artillerie at Vitry-le-Francois, comes from the research pool's account of Helene Gispert's study and of Montel's 1941 obituary; neither could be fetched. The pool tagged this attested in one array and reconstruction in the other, and the weaker tag is taken. Coordinate corrected to Nominatim's Vitry-le-Francois, 48.7262, 4.5852. Month and day default to January.
stops.campa: The war takes the analysis away and gives him arithmetic. With Paul Montel, his classmate from the rue d'Ulm, he works under the wartime inventions administration on the revision of artillery firing tables: trajectories computed, corrections tabulated, graphical charts drawn so that a gunner in a battery can read off an elevation without doing any mathematics at all. What formal position he held is disputed between the accounts and is not settled here. The town sits behind the Champagne front.
suggested_refs: The Centre d'etudes d'artillerie at Vitry-le-Francois; Helene Gispert's study of French mathematicians in the war (not fetched)
sources: Research dossier's account of Gispert (2024) and of Montel's 1941 obituary (neither verified)

stops.name: Paris, the divorce
stops.date_confidence: The year is attested (MacTutor: the marriage ended in divorce in 1916). The precise date of 3 November 1916 and the 11th-arrondissement venue come from an Oise civil-register marginal notation cited in the research pool and not re-verified, so both are treated as reconstruction; month and day default to January, and the stop takes the canonical Paris pin rather than the Mairie du 11e.
stops.campa: The marriage ends. Thirteen years, two children, a divorce, and no document reached says anything at all about the grounds, the arrangements, or where either of them lived afterwards. He is forty-one, in the middle of the war work, still a maître de conférences. Whatever this cost him he did not write down, or nobody has found what he wrote. Louise Marguerite Vallet leaves the record here and does not come back into it; the accounts that give her name give nothing else.
suggested_refs: The Paris divorce records for 1916, not located in this research
sources: Research dossier's citation of an Oise civil-register marginal notation (not verified)

stops.name: Paris, the break with Borel
stops.date_confidence: The dispute is attested (en.wikipedia: the disagreement with Emile Borel was published in the Annales scientifiques de l'Ecole normale superieure across 1918-1920). The particular volumes cited in the research pool, 35 (1918) and 37 (1920), were not re-fetched. The pin is the ENS, whose journal carried the exchange; it marks a publication and not a scene. Month and day default to January.
stops.campa: Borel had taught him, published him, and given him the countably additive measure of sets that the integral is built on. In 1918, writing while a Sorbonne chair stands vacant, Lebesgue publishes remarks on the theories of measure and integration; Borel answers; Lebesgue answers again. Each man holds that the other has understated what he did, and neither of them yields. The friendship does not survive it. The exchange runs in the Annales scientifiques de l'École normale supérieure until 1920.
suggested_refs: Lebesgue, 'Remarques sur les theories de la mesure et de l'integration', Annales scientifiques de l'ENS 35 (1918), and the exchange running to vol. 37 (1920)
sources: Research dossier's citation of the Annales exchange (issues not re-fetched)

stops.name: Paris, the chair at the Sorbonne
stops.date_confidence: Attested (MacTutor): promoted to professor of the application of geometry to analysis at the Sorbonne in 1918. No month or day is recorded; both default to January, which places this stop and the Borel stop in the same undated year. The research pool put the promotion at the end of 1918. Sorbonne pin inherited byte for byte, 48.8496, 2.3442.
stops.campa: At forty-three he is at last a professor at the Sorbonne, in a chair for the application of geometry to analysis. Eight years as maître de conférences, sixteen since the doctorate, and the appointment arrives inside the same twelve months as the public quarrel with the man who made the career possible. The Sorbonne took eighteen years to want him, and he holds its chair for three. They are the only three years of his life in which he is a full professor in a French university. In 1921 the Collège de France elects him and he goes.
suggested_refs: The Sorbonne chair of the application of geometry to analysis, held 1918-1921

stops.name: Paris, the chair of mathematics at the Collège de France
stops.date_confidence: The year is attested (MacTutor: professor of mathematics at the College de France, 1921-1941). The decree date of 31 July 1921 comes only from the research pool's citation of the College's Salamandre archive catalogue, which could not be fetched, so it is treated as reconstruction; month and day default to January.
stops.campa: He is elected to the chair of mathematics at the Collège de France, an institution with no students, no examinations and no degrees, where the professor lectures on his current work to whoever walks in off the street. It is the most complete freedom the French system offers a mathematician, and he holds it for twenty years, until he dies in it. What the chair gives him is time to teach the thing, argue it, and watch other men build on it. He is forty-six when he is elected, and there are no papers left in him of the kind he wrote at Nancy. Everything he will be remembered for was finished before he was thirty.
suggested_refs: The chair of mathematics at the College de France, 1921-1941; the College's Salamandre archive catalogue

stops.name: Paris, the inaugural lecture
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The date of 6 January 1922, and the content of the inaugural lecture on the College mathematicians Georges Humbert and Camille Jordan and on Roberval and Ramus, come from the research pool's citation of the printed lecture Les professeurs de mathematiques du College de France (1922). This was not independently fetched.
stops.campa: The inaugural lecture takes as its subject the mathematicians who held the chair before him. He speaks of Georges Humbert; of Camille Jordan, whose theory of content his own measure had swallowed and whose pages he had worked through in the school library twenty-five years earlier; and, further back, of Roberval and of Ramus. A man who spent his working life generalising other men's constructions opens his tenure by standing up and naming them. The lecture was printed the same year. Who was in the hall to hear it, no account reached records.
suggested_refs: Lebesgue, Les professeurs de mathematiques du College de France (1922), the printed inaugural lecture
sources: Research dossier's citation of the printed inaugural lecture (not verified)

stops.name: Paris, elected to the Académie des sciences
stops.date_confidence: Attested (MacTutor; en.wikipedia corroborates the year): elected to the Academie des sciences on 29 May 1922. The pin is the Institut de France, the Academie's seat. Nothing reached records the margin of the vote or the seat he took.
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of May the Académie des sciences elects him a member. He has been feeding it papers for twenty-one years, since the four pages came up from Nancy in 1901, and taking its prizes for ten: Houllevigue, Poncelet, Saintour, Petit d'Ormoy, four awards between 1912 and 1919 from a body that would not yet have him as a member. He is forty-six. The work came first, at twenty-six, and the institutions have arrived twenty years behind it. What the vote was, and whose seat he took, no source reached records.
suggested_refs: The election registers of the Academie des sciences, 29 May 1922

stops.name: Paris, the Notice sur les travaux scientifiques
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (MacTutor's list of major publications, also listed by en.wikipedia): Notice sur les travaux scientifiques de M. Henri Lebesgue, 1922, ninety-two pages. No month or day; both default to January, which puts it before the May election in the same year, although no source reached links the two documents. Canonical Paris pin, no place of composition being recorded.
stops.campa: He writes an account of his own scientific work, ninety-two pages of it, in the third person, in the form the French system requires of a candidate. It is a routine document, the thing a man submits when he is being considered for something. It is also the only continuous statement he ever made of what he thought he had done and in what order he had done it. Ninety-two pages about the mathematics, and in the third person, is the whole of what he chose to say about himself. He is his own biographer for the length of a pamphlet and then never again. After it there is no memoir, no autobiography, and no collected letters.
suggested_refs: Lebesgue, Notice sur les travaux scientifiques de M. Henri Lebesgue (1922), 92 pp.

stops.name: Sèvres, the school for women teachers
stops.date_confidence: Teaching at the Ecole normale superieure de Sevres is attested (MacTutor); the years are not pinned down in anything reached, and 1925 is a placeholder inside the 1920s, month and day defaulted. The account of his classroom manner comes from Lucienne Felix's and Paul Montel's testimony as relayed by the research pool and is not independently confirmed. Coordinate corrected: the school occupied the buildings of the old royal porcelain manufactory at Sevres, 48.8241, 2.2165, not the residential street given in the pool.
stops.campa: At Sèvres he teaches the women who will teach the girls of France, in the buildings of the old royal porcelain works. Those who sat in the room, writing it down long after he was dead, describe a course conducted as live investigation rather than recital. It is not the manner that gets a man a reputation as a lecturer, and it is not the manner of somebody who thinks mathematics is a finished object. He works the thing out in front of them, and when tiredness sends a calculation wrong he goes back and rebuilds it while they watch.
suggested_refs: The Ecole normale superieure de jeunes filles at Sevres, in the buildings of the ancienne Manufacture nationale
sources: Research dossier's citation of Lucienne Felix's and Paul Montel's testimony (not verified)

stops.name: Paris, the rue Vauquelin
stops.date_confidence: Attested (MacTutor): taught at the Ecole superieure de physique et de chimie industrielles de la Ville de Paris, 1927-1937. No month or day; both default to January. This appointment was absent from the research dossier altogether and was recovered from MacTutor during verification.
stops.campa: For ten years, alongside the Collège de France chair, he teaches at the municipal school of industrial physics and chemistry in the rue Vauquelin, a few hundred metres downhill from the rue d'Ulm. It is a school that trains engineers rather than theorists, and its teaching runs to the laboratory bench. The Collège pays him to lecture on whatever he is working on. This one pays him to teach a syllabus. He is fifty-two when he starts and sixty-two when he stops.
suggested_refs: The Ecole superieure de physique et de chimie industrielles, rue Vauquelin, Paris

stops.name: Paris, elected abroad
stops.date_confidence: The elections are attested: honorary member of the London Mathematical Society 1924 and Foreign Member of the Royal Society 1934 (MacTutor; Wikidata gives the exact date 3 May 1934 and the correct category, ForMemRS rather than Fellow); foreign associate of the Academie royale de Belgique on 6 June 1931 (MacTutor); Officer of the Legion d'honneur in 1932 (Wikidata Q206005), the August month given in the research pool being unsupported by anything reached. Nothing records Lebesgue travelling to London or Brussels for any of it, so the stop sits at the canonical Paris pin rather than staging him inside a building he may never have entered.
stops.campa: The foreign academies come for him in his fifties. The London Mathematical Society makes him an honorary member in 1924; the Royal Academy of Belgium elects him a foreign associate in June 1931; France makes him an Officer of the Legion of Honour in 1932; the Royal Society elects him a Foreign Member in May 1934. Whether he crossed the Channel or the Belgian border for any of it, no source reached says. A foreign member is generally elected in his absence and informed by letter.
suggested_refs: The Royal Society's Foreign Members register, 3 May 1934; the Academie royale de Belgique, rue Ducale, Brussels

stops.name: Paris, the tricycle to the Collège de France
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The account of the last course, taken from the memorial testimony of Lucienne Felix and Paul Montel as relayed by the research pool, could not be independently fetched. It is placed in the first months of 1941, under the occupation; month and day are defaulted for ordering only.
stops.campa: In the last winter he is too ill to walk to the Collège de France and hires a pedal tricycle to carry him there. Paris is occupied. He lectures on geometric constructions, and Lucienne Félix, who had been his student at Sèvres, sits in the room and takes it down; without her notebook the course would not exist at all. He is sixty-five, he has held the chair for twenty years, and he cannot get up the hill on his own legs. The account of all this comes from the people who were in the room, written down after he was dead. He gives the course.
suggested_refs: Lucienne Felix's notes of Lebesgue's last course on geometric constructions; the Denjoy-Felix-Montel memorial account (1957)
sources: Research dossier's synthesis of the Denjoy-Felix-Montel memorial account (not verified)

stops.name: Paris, the conics dictated from bed
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The dictation on conics to a student, Mlle Beauvallet, and the posthumous editing by Paul Montel come from the same memorial testimony and were not independently confirmed. The spring 1941 placement exists to order the segment and is not sourced; month and day are set for that purpose alone. Canonical Paris pin, no address being recorded.
stops.campa: When he can no longer get to the Collège he goes on working from bed, dictating material on the conic sections to a student, Mlle Beauvallet, who writes it down as he speaks. Conics are old mathematics, two thousand years old, and about as far from measure theory as a mathematician can get without leaving the subject. Nothing in the account suggests he thought of it as a last testament; it is the ordinary continuation of a working life, carried on horizontally because the alternative was to stop. Montel edits the material and publishes it after his death.
suggested_refs: The posthumous conics material, edited by Paul Montel
sources: Research dossier's synthesis of Felix's and Montel's testimony (not verified)

stops.name: Paris, the death
stops.date_confidence: Attested (MacTutor; en.wikipedia): died in Paris on 26 July 1941, aged 66. The 11th-arrondissement precision comes from the research pool and is confirmed by nothing else reached, so the stop takes the canonical Paris pin. No death certificate or contemporary medical diagnosis was located, and the tuberculosis commonly given as the cause is inherited from the family history rather than documented for him.
stops.campa: He dies in Paris on the twenty-sixth of July, sixty-six years old, in the second summer of the occupation. What killed him is not established: no certificate has been produced and no contemporary account names a disease. Tuberculosis is the recurrent attribution, and tuberculosis is what took his father and both his sisters when he was three, which makes it plausible without making it documented. He had been ill for years. That is as far as the record goes.
suggested_refs: The Paris death registers for July 1941, not located in this research

stops.name: Gouvieux, the grave that cannot be confirmed
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and weakly so. Wikidata Q206005 gives the place of burial as the old cemetery of Gouvieux in the Oise at 49.189605, 2.430681, and the coordinate here is that figure rounded, the research pool having mis-transcribed it as 2.4251. But the reference attached to the Wikidata claim, a page of L'Enseignement Mathematique vol. 38, does not on inspection contain the word Gouvieux or any burial detail, and Nominatim finds no cemetery of that name in the commune. No funeral notice or cemetery register was located. The burial date of 28 July exists only to order the segment and is not sourced at all.
stops.campa: The single record of where he was put names a cemetery at Gouvieux, in the Oise, forty miles from the house in Beauvais where he was born. He measured scattered sets of points for a living, and his grave cannot presently be located. The reference attached to that record turns out not to mention Gouvieux, or a burial, or him; the cemetery it names cannot be found under that name in the commune. No funeral notice has been produced, no register entry, and no photograph of a stone.
suggested_refs: Wikidata Q206005, property P119; L'Enseignement Mathematique vol. 38, the page cited there and found not to support the claim
sources: e-periodica.ch, L'Enseignement Mathematique 38 (checked, does not corroborate)

stops.name: Paris, what the integral turned out to be for
stops.date_confidence: The Wiener claim is attested (en.wikipedia, 'Henri Lebesgue'): in 1947 Norbert Wiener argued that Lebesgue's integral had unexpected but important implications for the foundations Willard Gibbs laid under statistical mechanics. The original Wiener text was not checked. The abstraction of Lebesgue's measure into general spaces by Frechet, Daniell, Radon and Caratheodory is carried from the research dossier and not independently verified. Month and day default to January; the pin is the canonical Paris pin, this stop marking the afterlife of a body of work rather than a place anyone stood.
stops.campa: Fréchet, Daniell, Radon and Carathéodory lift the measure off the Euclidean line and set it on abstract spaces, where it becomes the language probability is written in. In 1947 Norbert Wiener argues that the integral a schoolmaster built at Nancy has unexpected consequences for the foundations Willard Gibbs laid under statistical mechanics. None of this is what it was made for. It was made to say when a limit could be carried inside an integral sign.
suggested_refs: Norbert Wiener's 1947 argument on the Lebesgue integral and the Gibbs foundations of statistical mechanics
sources: Research dossier on the Frechet-Daniell-Radon-Caratheodory abstraction (not independently verified)

stops.name: Beauvais, the street, and the crater
stops.date_confidence: The rue Henri Lebesgue in Beauvais is confirmed by OpenStreetMap geocoding at 49.42025, 2.07941; the date of the naming is not established anywhere reached, and 1975 is a bare placeholder with month and day defaulted. The lunar crater Lebesgue, 11.39 km across at 5.14 S 88.97 E on the far side, was approved by the IAU in 1976 (USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature, feature 3323). Asteroid 26908 Lebesgue, provisional designation 1996 GK, was discovered on 11 April 1996 by P. G. Comba at Prescott (NASA/JPL Small-Body Database).
stops.campa: Beauvais gives a street his name, in the south of the town, well away from the rue de la Madeleine where the house stood. When the naming happened nobody has recorded. His name is also on a crater eleven kilometres across on the far side of the Moon, approved in 1976, and on an asteroid found at Prescott, Arizona, in 1996 and numbered 26908. Nothing in Beauvais marks the birth house, because nobody knows which house it was. The citation written for the asteroid puts the case for him in a single clause.
stops.quote: generalization of the Riemann integral revolutionized the field of integration and has played a fundamental role in modern analysis
stops.quote_source: Naming citation for asteroid 26908 Lebesgue (1996 GK), NASA/JPL Small-Body Database, honouring Henri-Leon Lebesgue (1875-1941) of the College de France.
suggested_refs: Lunar crater Lebesgue, IAU 1976, USGS Gazetteer feature 3323; asteroid 26908 Lebesgue (1996 GK)

stops.name: Rennes, the plaque and the centre
stops.date_confidence: The plaque to Henri-Leon Lebesgue at 4 rue Pongerard in Rennes is attested by a photograph of 21 May 2023 on Wikimedia Commons; the plaque itself is undated. The Centre Henri Lebesgue exists and, by its own site at lebesgue.fr, federates mathematics across six cities in western France including Rennes, Nantes, Brest, Angers and Le Mans; the founding year of 2012 is not stated by that site nor by the Wikipedia page cited for it in the research pool, so it is reconstruction and is used here only to order the stop. The Annales Henri Lebesgue, owned by the ENS Rennes and hosted by Centre Mersenne, carries no confirmed volume-one year: the 2018 usually given rests on a copyright line.
stops.campa: In the town where he spent four years waiting for Paris, a plaque goes up at 4 rue Pongérard on a house he lived in. Rennes has kept him better than Paris has. His name is on a mathematics network that federates the laboratories of six cities in the west of France, and on an open-access journal published from the École normale supérieure of Rennes, free to read and free to publish in. He got through school himself on other people's charity. The plaque carries no date, and nothing reached says what year it went up.
suggested_refs: The plaque at 4 rue Pongerard, Rennes, photographed 21 May 2023; the Centre Henri Lebesgue (lebesgue.fr); the Annales Henri Lebesgue (annales.lebesgue.fr)
